name: Amiloxate
lead: Amiloxate (isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate, isopentyl 4-methoxycinnamate, IMC) is a cinnamate ester used as a UVB filter in sunscreen products [1]. For appearance, sunscreen filters like it are used to limit UV exposure that causes sunburn, tanning, uneven pigmentation and visible photoaging, so skin keeps a smoother, more even look over time [13]. Amiloxate has been approved in the European Union since 1997; in the United States it has been under regulatory evaluation rather than listed as an approved sunscreen active [1].

Published literature on amiloxate itself consists mainly of analytical methods, environmental occurrence studies, and photoallergy reports [2][7][10]. It is chemically close to octinoxate, the better-known cinnamate UVB filter [1].
infobox: Under evaluation (not an approved OTC active)

paras: Amiloxate is the 3-methylbutyl ester of 4-methoxycinnamic acid, with formula C15H20O3 and a molar mass of about 248 g/mol [1]. Like other organic ('chemical') filters, it is an aromatic molecule that absorbs high-energy ultraviolet light and releases the energy as lower-energy radiation, so less UV reaches the skin [13]. It sits in the UVB filter group alongside other cinnamates such as octinoxate [1][13]. Cinnamates as a class are known to cause allergic contact dermatitis in some people, as filters and as excipients [13].

Amiloxate appears among the UV filters measured in commercial suncare formulations and cosmetics by chromatography methods [2][3][4]. In a mouse inflammation assay of the 21 UV filters then authorised in Europe, 13 showed anti-inflammatory effects; researchers proposed this might explain differences between in vivo and in vitro SPF measurements [5].

The EU approved amiloxate in 1997 under its cosmetics framework, where sunscreen is treated as a cosmetic [1][13]. In the US sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, which makes approval of newer ingredients slower and narrows the ingredient list; amiloxate has been described as undergoing regulatory evaluation there [1][13]. In 2021 the FDA sorted filters into categories, and as of that year only zinc oxide and titanium dioxide were listed as generally recognised as safe and effective [13].

A 15-year review of sunscreen allergy found that 20% of 402 patients tested had allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis to one or more UV absorbers [6]. A case report described photoallergic contact dermatitis due to isoamyl p-methoxycinnamate in a sunscreen marketed as organic [7], and another study reported photoallergy to UV filters across several sunscreens [8].

Amiloxate has been measured in indoor dust [9] and in a freshwater recreational reservoir, where researchers examined its dissipation [10]. Porcine-skin work found chemical UV absorbers largely remained in the outer stratum corneum in a barrier-mimetic formulation [11].

No clinical trials specific to amiloxate were found. It was among the filters evaluated in a registered multicentre European photopatch study (1,000 participants) [12], and in the allergy series described above [6].

Amiloxate has little visibility in skincare communities, where discussion of UV filters centres on better-known ones such as octinoxate, oxybenzone, avobenzone and mineral filters. Public-health bodies generally hold that skin cancer risk from sun exposure outweighs the unproven concerns about approved filters, per Wikipedia's sunscreen article [13].

timeline.event: The FDA's administrative order sorted sunscreen filters into three categories [13].

card.summary: Cinnamate UVB sunscreen filter approved in the EU since 1997; photoallergy case reports exist and little else is studied.
card.note: Not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.

quick.overview:
Amiloxate is a cinnamate-type UVB filter used in some sunscreens, approved in the EU since 1997.

Published work on it is mostly analytical and environmental, plus case reports of photoallergic contact dermatitis.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB radiation within the sunscreen film.
quick.risks: Photoallergic contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not an approved US OTC sunscreen active.

chain: Absorbs UVB radiation in a sunscreen
Less sunburn and photodamage, supporting even tone and smoother skin over years
angle.text: Amiloxate is one of the organic ingredients that lets a sunscreen absorb UVB. People who use sunscreen to keep their skin looking even and youthful rely on filters of this kind, though few products today list amiloxate specifically.
